claims.text: Spray-drying followed by a well-timed secondary thermal decomposition-reduction step enables nearly simultaneous nucleation and reduction of all noble-metal precursor species.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation and reduction enforce atomic-level mixing.
Atomic-level mixing suppresses phase separation and elemental segregation in noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
The initial precursor contains noble-metal ions, notably Pt and Ru in varying proportions.
The synthesis forms uniformly distributed nucleation sites within precursor droplets.
The uniformly distributed nucleation sites anchor simultaneous reduction of all metal species.
Rapid secondary heating forces all metal species to reduce concurrently.
Concurrent reduction freezes a high-entropy configuration before diffusion-driven segregation or phase separation occurs.
Slower processes develop thermal gradients that permit elemental migration and segregation.
The timed secondary-heating route will produce homogeneously alloyed nanoparticles with uniformly mixed surface atoms.
Delaying or omitting the controlled secondary-heating step will produce more phase separation and less uniform morphology.
Extended diffusion time causes elemental segregation, phase separation, or uncontrolled morphology.
The proposed mechanism should apply to noble-metal systems having suitable mutual miscibility under rapid-reduction conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when precursors inherently favor segregation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when different precursor species require incompatible thermal reduction conditions.
Failure of controlled secondary heating to improve homogeneity relative to a delayed or omitted secondary-heating baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
